concepts.title: Conceptual, logical and physical models
concepts.kw: conceptual model logical model physical model entities attributes relationships erd entity relationship diagram cardinality ddl abstraction levels
concepts.s: Data models are drawn at three levels: conceptual for business entities, logical for attributes and keys, and physical for actual tables in a specific database.
concepts.d: A conceptual model names the main business entities and how they relate, such as Customer places Order, and is agreed with business stakeholders. A logical model adds attributes, primary and foreign keys, cardinality (one-to-many, many-to-many) and normalisation, but stays independent of any database product. A physical model turns that into real tables, data types, indexes, partitions and constraints for a specific platform, such as Snowflake or PostgreSQL, and can be generated as DDL. Moving through the levels keeps business meaning separate from technical choices, so one logical model can have different physical designs.
concepts.e: Conceptual: Shipment, Carrier and Stop, where a shipment has many stops. Logical: Shipment(shipment_id PK, carrier_id FK, mode), Stop(stop_id PK, shipment_id FK, sequence). Physical: a Snowflake table clustered by ship_date with NUMBER(38,0) keys.
concepts.c: Why keep the logical model independent of the database you'll use?
concepts.i: Architecture interviews ask you to sketch a model at each level for a domain and explain who each level is for.

concepts.title: Data Vault 2.0
concepts.kw: data vault 2.0 hubs links satellites business keys hash keys raw vault business vault point in time bridge tables auditability insert only
concepts.s: Data Vault is a modelling method for the integration layer of an enterprise warehouse, built from hubs, links and satellites so new sources can be added without remodelling.
concepts.d: Hubs hold unique business keys, such as customer number, with load date and source. Links hold relationships between hubs, such as a customer placing an order. Satellites hold descriptive attributes and their history, attached to a hub or link, with a new row whenever values change. Version 2.0 uses hash keys so tables can load in parallel, and loads are insert-only, which makes the model fully auditable. The raw vault keeps source data as delivered, the business vault adds derived rules, and point-in-time and bridge tables help querying. Star schemas are usually built on top for reporting, because the vault itself is awkward to query.
concepts.e: Adding a second order system means a new satellite on the existing Order hub with that system's attributes. The hub, links and earlier satellites don't change.
concepts.c: Why are star schemas usually built on top of a Data Vault rather than replacing it?
concepts.i: Senior architecture interviews ask you to explain hubs, links and satellites, and when Data Vault is worth its complexity.

concepts.title: One big table and wide-table modelling
concepts.kw: one big table obt wide tables denormalised denormalized flattened columnar warehouse fewer joins dashboards performance redundancy
concepts.s: One big table (OBT) modelling flattens facts and their dimension attributes into a single wide table, trading storage and some flexibility for simple, fast queries.
concepts.d: Columnar warehouses compress repeated values well and only read the columns a query needs, so a wide table with hundreds of columns is cheap to query. Analysts and BI tools avoid writing joins, and dashboards run faster. The costs: dimension changes require rebuilding the table, attribute history is fixed at load time, definitions can be duplicated across many wide tables, and the table can grow very large. A common pattern keeps a star schema as the governed core and builds wide tables from it for specific uses, such as a dashboard or a machine learning feature table.
concepts.e: An orders_wide table joins order items with customer, product, store and promotion attributes into 140 columns. The sales dashboard queries it with no joins and loads in 2 seconds instead of 9.
concepts.c: Why are wide tables cheaper on columnar warehouses than on row-based databases?
concepts.i: Expect to compare one big table with star schemas and say when you'd use each.

concepts.title: Semantic and metrics layers
concepts.kw: semantic layer metrics layer dbt semantic layer metricflow cube lookml looker measures dimensions single source of truth consistent metrics governed definitions
concepts.s: A semantic layer defines business metrics and dimensions once, in code, so every dashboard, notebook and AI tool computes "revenue" or "active customer" the same way.
concepts.d: Without it, each BI tool and analyst rewrites metric logic in SQL, and numbers drift apart. A semantic layer maps business terms to tables and joins, and defines measures, such as net revenue as the sum of item amounts minus returns and discounts, with their filters, time grains and allowed dimensions. Tools query the layer, and it generates the SQL. Examples include the dbt Semantic Layer with MetricFlow, Cube, LookML in Looker, and semantic models in Power BI. It also enables access control on metrics and gives LLM assistants governed definitions to query instead of guessing.
concepts.e: Finance and marketing reported different monthly revenue because one excluded cancelled orders. Defining net_revenue once in the semantic layer made both dashboards show Rs 4.82 crore.
concepts.c: Why does a semantic layer help when teams use several BI tools?
concepts.i: Expect to explain the problem it solves, how metrics are defined, and how it fits with dbt and BI tools.

concepts.title: Master data management
concepts.kw: master data management mdm golden record customer master product master matching merging survivorship data stewardship hub registry
concepts.s: Master data management creates one trusted, shared version of core entities such as customers, products, suppliers and locations across many systems.
concepts.d: The same customer or supplier often exists in the ERP, CRM, TMS and e-commerce systems with different ids and spellings. MDM matches records that refer to the same entity, using exact and fuzzy rules on names, addresses, phone numbers and tax ids such as GSTIN, merges them, and applies survivorship rules to choose the best value for each attribute, producing a golden record. Styles include registry (only cross-references ids), consolidation (a read-only golden copy), and centralised hubs that author master data. Data stewards resolve uncertain matches, and governance defines ownership and quality rules.
concepts.e: "Sharma Traders Pvt Ltd" in SAP and "Sharma Traders" in the TMS share a GSTIN, so MDM merges them into one supplier golden record, keeping SAP's bank details and the TMS's latest contact phone by survivorship rules.
concepts.c: What are survivorship rules, and why are they needed?
concepts.i: Senior roles ask how you'd design customer or product mastering, matching rules and stewardship.

concepts.title: Modern data stack reference architecture
concepts.kw: modern data stack reference architecture ingestion fivetran airbyte warehouse snowflake bigquery dbt transformation bi orchestration reverse etl observability catalog
concepts.s: The modern data stack is a set of cloud services, each doing one job, that together move data from sources to analytics: ingest, store, transform, serve and govern.
concepts.d: A typical reference architecture: managed connectors such as Fivetran or Airbyte, plus CDC and event streams, ingest data; a cloud warehouse or lakehouse such as Snowflake, BigQuery or Databricks stores it; dbt transforms it in layers; an orchestrator such as Airflow or Dagster schedules the work; BI tools and a semantic layer serve it; reverse ETL sends results back to operational tools. Cross-cutting pieces include a catalog, observability, access control and cost monitoring. The benefits are speed and low operations effort; the risks are tool sprawl, overlapping costs and integration gaps between many vendors.
concepts.e: A D2C brand runs Airbyte to load Shopify, Razorpay and Meta Ads data into BigQuery, dbt models on top, Looker dashboards, and Hightouch syncing customer segments back to its email tool.
concepts.c: What's the main risk of assembling a stack from many separate tools?
concepts.i: Expect to draw a reference architecture, name a tool per layer, and justify the choices for a given company size.

concepts.title: Cloud data platforms compared: AWS, Azure and GCP
concepts.kw: aws azure gcp cloud platforms comparison s3 adls gcs redshift synapse fabric bigquery glue data factory dataflow kinesis event hubs pubsub
concepts.s: AWS, Azure and Google Cloud offer equivalent building blocks for data platforms under different names, and the right choice usually depends on the organisation more than on features.
concepts.d: Object storage: S3, ADLS Gen2 and Google Cloud Storage. Warehouses: Redshift, Azure Synapse and Microsoft Fabric, and BigQuery. Integration: Glue, Data Factory and Dataflow or Dataproc. Streaming: Kinesis or MSK, Event Hubs, and Pub/Sub. Managed Spark: EMR, Databricks on Azure, and Dataproc. Choice drivers are existing contracts and skills, identity (Azure suits Microsoft 365 shops), data residency regions in India, the ecosystem of the source systems, pricing and credits. Many companies use Snowflake or Databricks across clouds to reduce lock-in, and some are multi-cloud by acquisition rather than design.
concepts.e: A manufacturer on SAP and Microsoft 365 chooses Azure: ADLS for the lake, Data Factory for SAP extraction, Databricks for processing and Power BI for reporting, all using Entra ID for access.
concepts.c: What are the equivalent object storage services on AWS, Azure and GCP?
concepts.i: Expect to map services across clouds and explain how you'd recommend a platform for a client.

concepts.title: Separating storage and compute
concepts.kw: separation of storage and compute decoupled elastic scaling object storage independent compute clusters workload isolation shared data serverless
concepts.s: Modern data platforms keep data in cheap, durable storage and run compute separately, so each can scale and be paid for independently.
concepts.d: In older warehouses and Hadoop clusters, storage and compute lived on the same machines, so adding storage meant buying compute and vice versa, and every workload competed for the same cluster. Decoupled platforms store data in object storage or managed storage and spin up compute clusters on demand. Benefits: elastic scaling, paying for compute only while it runs, isolating workloads (ELT, BI, data science) on separate clusters over the same data, and using several engines on one copy with open table formats. Trade-offs: network latency to storage, which caching and pruning offset, and the need for cost controls on easily created compute.
concepts.e: Month-end finance queries get their own large warehouse for three days, then shrink back, while daily ELT and BI warehouses run unaffected on the same tables.
concepts.c: How does separating storage and compute help with workload isolation?
concepts.i: Expect to explain the benefits and trade-offs, and how Snowflake, BigQuery and lakehouses implement it.

concepts.title: Real-time analytics architecture
concepts.kw: real-time analytics architecture streaming olap clickhouse druid pinot kafka flink low latency dashboards freshness seconds materialized views
concepts.s: Real-time analytics answers questions on data that is seconds old, which needs streaming ingestion, fast analytical stores and careful choices about what really must be real time.
concepts.d: Events flow through Kafka or a similar log; stream processors such as Flink enrich and aggregate them; results land in a real-time OLAP store such as ClickHouse, Apache Druid or Apache Pinot, built for fast aggregations over fresh data and many concurrent users. Some warehouses also offer streaming ingestion and incrementally refreshed materialised views. Design for late and duplicate events, decide the freshness each use really needs, and pre-aggregate where possible. Real time costs more to build and run than batch, so reserve it for operational decisions such as fraud, dispatch or live order tracking.
concepts.e: A quick commerce control room shows orders, rider availability and delivery times per dark store with 5-second freshness: Kafka feeds Flink, which writes per-minute aggregates to ClickHouse for the dashboards.
concepts.c: How would you decide whether a dashboard really needs real-time data?
concepts.i: Senior architecture interviews ask you to design a real-time dashboard end to end and justify its latency and cost.

concepts.title: Reverse ETL and operational analytics
concepts.kw: reverse etl operational analytics hightouch census sync warehouse to crm salesforce marketing tools activation customer segments data activation
concepts.s: Reverse ETL copies modelled data from the warehouse back into operational tools such as CRM, marketing and support systems, so teams act on it where they work.
concepts.d: Analytics often produces valuable results, such as churn risk, lifetime value or product-qualified leads, that stay in dashboards. Reverse ETL tools such as Hightouch and Census, or custom jobs, sync selected warehouse tables to Salesforce, HubSpot, ad platforms or support tools on a schedule, mapping columns to fields and sending only changed rows. Treat syncs like production pipelines: define keys and field mappings carefully, respect API rate limits, handle failures and deletions, and monitor them. Watch for consent and privacy rules when sending personal data to third parties.
concepts.e: Every hour, customers with churn risk above 0.7 and lifetime value above Rs 20,000 sync to the support tool, so agents see a "high-value, at risk" flag on incoming tickets.
concepts.c: Why should reverse ETL sync only changed rows rather than the full table each time?
concepts.i: Expect to explain where reverse ETL fits in the stack, its use cases and its operational risks.

questions.q: What's the difference between conceptual, logical and physical data models?

p.t: Physical: tables, types and indexes for a platform
Each level has a different audience

questions.a: A conceptual model shows the main business entities and relationships, like Customer places Order, with no technical detail. A logical model adds attributes, primary and foreign keys, cardinality and normalisation, but stays independent of any database product. A physical model implements it for a specific platform: tables, data types, indexes, partitions and constraints. Each level has a different audience: business stakeholders for conceptual, analysts and architects for logical, and engineers and DBAs for physical.

questions.q: How would you take a new business domain from conceptual to physical model?

p.t: Workshops to agree entities and definitions

questions.a: Start with workshops with business experts to agree the entities, their definitions and how they relate, which becomes the conceptual model. Then identify business keys, attributes and relationships with cardinality, and normalise in the logical model to remove redundancy. The physical design then fits the workload and platform: denormalising into star schemas for analytics, choosing types, partition and clustering keys, and constraints. Finally, review the models with stakeholders and version them in Git or a modelling tool so changes are traceable.

questions.q: Explain hubs, links and satellites in Data Vault.

p.t: Star schemas on top for reporting

questions.a: Hubs hold the unique business keys of core entities, such as customer number, with load date and record source. Links hold relationships between hubs, such as customer to order, and can join several hubs. Satellites hold the descriptive attributes and their history, adding a row whenever values change. Data Vault 2.0 uses hash keys so loads can run in parallel, and loads are insert-only, so everything is auditable. Because it's awkward to query directly, star schemas are built on top for reporting.

questions.q: When is Data Vault worth its complexity, and when isn't it?

p.t: Not worth it for small or simple platforms

questions.a: It's worth it in large enterprises integrating many source systems whose structures change, where adding a source shouldn't mean remodelling, and where regulators need auditability and full history, such as banks and insurers. It also lets parallel teams load incrementally. It isn't worth it for small or simple platforms with a few stable sources, where it's overkill and a star schema built with dbt is faster to deliver. Done well, it needs automation tools to generate the many tables, and skills in the team.

questions.q: Compare one big table modelling with a star schema.

p.t: Wide table flattens facts and dimensions
Harder to change and duplicates definitions
Common pattern: star core, wide tables on top

questions.a: One big table flattens facts and dimension attributes into a single wide table, so users need no joins and dashboards are faster and simpler. Columnar storage makes it cheap, since repeated values compress well and only queried columns are read. But dimension changes mean rebuilding it, history is fixed at load time, and definitions get duplicated across wide tables. A star schema is more flexible and governed. The common pattern keeps a star schema as the governed core, with wide tables built from it for specific dashboards or ML features.

questions.q: A dashboard on a star schema is slow because of many joins. What are your options?

p.t: Build a wide or aggregated table for it
Check the queries the tool generates

questions.a: First check the generated SQL and query plan, since BI tools often produce inefficient queries. Then options: build a wide table or an aggregate table at the dashboard's grain, such as daily sales by store, refreshed by the pipeline; use materialised views where the warehouse supports them; tune clustering and partitioning on the fact table so filters prune data; or use BI extracts and caching. I'd pick the simplest option that meets the response time.

questions.q: What problem does a semantic layer solve, and how does it work?

p.t: Tools query the layer, which generates SQL
Examples: dbt Semantic Layer, Cube, LookML

questions.a: It solves inconsistent metrics: when every dashboard and analyst writes their own SQL, teams report different numbers for the same metric. A semantic layer has measures and dimensions defined once, in code: how revenue is calculated, its filters, joins and allowed time grains. Tools query the layer by metric name and it generates the SQL. Examples are the dbt Semantic Layer with MetricFlow, Cube and LookML. It also adds governed access to metrics and gives LLM assistants trusted definitions to use.

questions.q: Finance and marketing report different revenue numbers. How would you fix it for good?

p.t: Encode it in a semantic layer or shared model
Point dashboards at the governed metric

questions.a: First find the definitional differences, such as one team excluding cancelled orders or using order date instead of delivery date. Then agree one owner and one definition, possibly with clearly named variants like gross and net revenue. Encode it once, in a semantic layer or a shared dbt model, and point every dashboard at the governed metric rather than custom SQL. Document it in the catalog and add tests, such as reconciling monthly totals with the finance ledger.

questions.q: How does master data management create a golden record?

p.t: Match records with exact and fuzzy rules
Publish the golden record and cross-references

questions.a: It collects records for the entity from source systems such as ERP, CRM and TMS, then standardises them. Matching uses exact and fuzzy rules on names, addresses, phones and tax ids such as GSTIN to find records for the same entity. Matched records are merged, and survivorship rules choose each attribute's best value, such as the most recent phone or the ERP's bank details. Data stewards resolve uncertain matches. The golden record is published with cross-references to each source id.

questions.q: Compare registry, consolidation and centralised MDM styles.

p.t: Consolidation builds a read-only golden copy

questions.a: Registry style keeps data in the sources and only maintains a cross-reference of matching ids, which is lightest but gives limited quality control. Consolidation builds a read-only golden copy for analytics, without changing sources. Centralised, or hub, style makes the MDM hub where master data is authored, then pushes it to systems, giving the most control but needing the most effort and process change. I'd choose by maturity and need, often starting with consolidation for analytics.

questions.q: Draw a modern data stack for a mid-size e-commerce company and justify each layer.

p.t: BI, semantic layer and reverse ETL

questions.a: Ingestion with managed connectors like Fivetran or Airbyte for SaaS sources, plus CDC for the order database. A cloud warehouse such as BigQuery or Snowflake, since a mid-size team wants low operations effort. dbt for transformations in layers with tests. An orchestrator such as Airflow or Dagster to schedule and order the work. BI tools on a semantic layer for consistent metrics, and reverse ETL to push segments to marketing tools. Across it, a catalog, observability and cost monitoring.

questions.q: What are the downsides of the modern data stack, and how do you manage them?
questions.a: Tool sprawl: many tools with integration gaps between them, each needing skills and maintenance. Costs add up across vendors, often charged by rows or credits that grow quickly. Governance and lineage get fragmented across tools. I'd manage it by consolidating where possible, choosing fewer tools that cover more layers, giving each tool clear ownership, and doing cost tracking per tool and team with regular reviews of what's actually used.

questions.q: Map the main data services across AWS, Azure and GCP.

p.t: Warehouses: Redshift, Synapse or Fabric, BigQuery

questions.a: Object storage: S3 on AWS, ADLS Gen2 on Azure, and GCS on Google Cloud. Warehouses: Redshift, Synapse or Microsoft Fabric, and BigQuery. Integration and ETL: Glue, Data Factory, and Dataflow. Streaming: Kinesis or MSK, Event Hubs, and Pub/Sub. Managed Spark: EMR, Azure Databricks, and Dataproc. Snowflake and Databricks also run on all three.

questions.q: How would you recommend a cloud platform for a client's new data platform?
questions.a: I'd start with the client: existing contracts, credits and team skills often decide it. Then identity and ecosystem fit: a Microsoft 365 and SAP shop integrates well with Azure, while a Google Workspace digital business may suit GCP. Check data residency needs and that Indian regions offer the services required. Look at source systems and available connectors. Then compare cost for a realistic workload and the lock-in risk, where Snowflake or Databricks and open formats keep options open.

questions.q: What are the benefits and trade-offs of separating storage and compute?

p.t: Pay for compute only while running
Isolate workloads on the same data

questions.a: Storage and compute scale independently, so you don't buy servers to hold more data. You pay for compute only while it runs and can resize it per job. Workloads such as ELT, BI and data science are isolated on separate clusters over the same data, so they don't slow each other down. With open table formats, several engines can work on one copy. Trade-offs: network latency to object storage, which caching and pruning offset, and runaway costs because compute is so easy to create, so you need auto-suspend and budgets.

questions.q: How do Snowflake, BigQuery and a lakehouse each separate storage and compute?

p.t: Snowflake: managed storage plus virtual warehouses
Lakehouse: open files on object storage
Spark or SQL clusters as compute

questions.a: Snowflake keeps data in its managed storage on cloud object storage and runs queries on virtual warehouses you size and suspend. BigQuery is serverless: storage is managed and queries use slots allocated automatically or reserved. A lakehouse stores open files, such as Delta or Iceberg tables, on your own object storage, and any compute engine, like Spark clusters or SQL engines such as Trino, reads them.

questions.q: Design a real-time operations dashboard for a quick commerce company.

p.t: Event streams from apps and systems into Kafka
Stream processing for enrichment and aggregation
Freshness targets and cost per use case

questions.a: Order, rider and inventory events from the apps and backend systems flow into Kafka. Flink enriches them with store and zone data and aggregates per store per minute, such as open orders and average delivery time. Results go into a real-time OLAP store such as ClickHouse, Druid or Pinot, which serves dashboards with many concurrent users in milliseconds. The design handles late and duplicate events with event time, watermarks and idempotent keys. I'd set freshness targets per metric, seconds for rider availability and minutes for others, to keep cost down.

questions.q: Stakeholders want everything real time. How do you push back?

p.t: Ask what decision the data drives
Reserve streaming for operational use cases

questions.a: I'd ask what decision each metric drives and how quickly someone can act on it. If a manager reviews a report each morning, hourly data is plenty. Real time costs more to build, run and support, and is more complex to keep correct. So match freshness to the decision, offer near real time options like 5 to 15 minute micro-batch loads where they're good enough, and reserve true streaming for operational cases such as fraud checks, dispatch or live tracking.

questions.q: What is reverse ETL, and what would you use it for?

p.t: Sync warehouse data back to operational tools
Use cases: CRM fields, segments, scores
Tools such as Hightouch and Census
Field mappings and changed rows only

questions.a: Reverse ETL syncs modelled warehouse data back to operational tools, so teams act on it where they work. Uses include CRM fields like lifetime value, customer segments for marketing audiences, and churn or lead scores for sales and support. Tools such as Hightouch and Census handle field mapping and send changed rows only on a schedule. I'd treat syncs as production pipelines: tested, with alerts, and monitored for failures.

questions.q: What can go wrong with reverse ETL, and how do you prevent it?

p.t: API rate limits and partial failures
Privacy and consent for personal data

questions.a: Syncs can overwrite fields users edited in the CRM, so agree which system owns each field. Destination APIs have rate limits, and partial failures leave some records out of date, so syncs need retries and reconciliation. Deletes and key mismatches can create duplicates or orphaned records, so use stable keys. Personal data sent to third-party tools must respect privacy rules and consent. And syncs need monitoring and alerts like any pipeline.
